summary: Glass Wall Systems designs, makes and installs the outside surfaces of buildings, including glass walls, covering panels and ventilation slats.
description: Picture an office tower with glass across its exterior. Those panels need supporting frames, connections and careful fitting. Glass Wall Systems works on this outer surface, called the façade or building envelope. It does not have to construct the entire tower to supply this part of it.
money: A project customer pays for the agreed design, materials, manufacturing and installation work. The company pays for glass, aluminium and other materials, factory workers, transport, site labour and running costs. Delays, repairs or unpaid bills can reduce what remains.
customers: Real-estate developers, hospitals, airport authorities, building contractors and companies putting up offices, homes or institutional buildings in India. Overseas, the company also sells made-to-order façade parts to façade contractors in the USA and Australia, who fit them on site. Each customer pays for its specified exterior work. An apartment purchaser or a hotel guest normally uses the finished building rather than directly buying the façade contract.
drivers: Winning workable contracts, obtaining materials, making panels, getting access to the building site, fitting them correctly and receiving customer payment.

groups.title: Glass walls on the outside of buildings
groups.explanation: A curtain wall is an outer wall that encloses the building without carrying the main weight of its floors and structure. Glass and frames must be designed for the project and fitted to the building correctly.

groups.title: Other outside coverings and slats
groups.examples: Cladding, louvers and related exterior parts.
groups.explanation: Cladding means panels or other material covering the outside. Louvers are angled slats used in openings for purposes such as ventilation or screening. The contract specifies which materials and performance the customer needs.

groups.title: Planning the exterior before making it
groups.explanation: Engineers turn the architect’s appearance and the project’s requirements into parts that can be made and fitted. They work out the connections and check how their work meets the rest of the building.

groups.title: Making and fitting the parts
groups.examples: Factory fabrication, delivery and site installation.
groups.explanation: Fabrication means making or assembling the parts. For Indian projects, workers prepare panels in the factory, transport them and fit them at the building. For customers in the USA and Australia, the company makes and ships the parts and a local contractor fits them. Factory completion alone does not finish the customer’s project.

groups.title: Windows, doors and skylights for expensive homes
groups.examples: Custom windows, doors, skylights and partition walls, mainly through its subsidiary Yes Systems.
groups.explanation: Fenestration is the industry word for windows, doors and other openings in a building. A subsidiary is a company owned by Glass Wall Systems; Yes Systems was bought during the year to March 2026 and fits these products in homes and commercial buildings. It is smaller than the façade work in the offer document’s figures.

basics.title: The customer can buy one combined job
basics.text: Design, manufacturing and installation can be stages of the same contract. They explain the work, but they are not automatically separate businesses with separately published profits.

basics.title: A completed panel is not a collected payment
basics.text: The company may make parts while waiting for access to the site. The customer can require checks of completed work before approving a bill. The company must still pay workers and suppliers during the wait.

steps.title: Agree and draw the required exterior
steps.text: Confirm materials, appearance, connections, responsibilities and how completed work will be checked.

steps.title: Buy materials and make the parts
steps.text: Arrange glass, aluminium and other items, then cut, process or assemble the required components.

steps.title: Deliver and install when the site is ready
steps.text: Move parts to the building and fit them safely as the project allows. Inspect and correct work as needed.

steps.title: Obtain approval, bill and collect
steps.text: Have the customer confirm completed work, send bills under the contract and collect payment. Some money may be held back until later conditions are met.

specifics.title: The customer’s building schedule affects this supplier
specifics.text: If the building is not ready for installation, finished panels can wait in storage and workers or equipment may wait too. An order for a tower exterior does not mean the full contract is immediately earned.

specifics.title: Some payment can be held back
specifics.text: Retention means money the customer keeps until agreed completion or defect conditions have been satisfied. Physical work can therefore finish before the company receives every payment.

specifics.title: Work, billing and collection do not always happen together
specifics.text: The accounts can record work performed before it can be billed without further conditions; this is called a contract asset. Receivables are customer amounts due. Neither label means the money is already in the bank.

watch: Are signed projects becoming installed exterior walls?
Orders still need ready sites, materials and workers.
Read completion schedules and progress on the work already accepted. Check design approvals, site access and installation resources rather than treating every announced order as current sales.
Who pays if materials or the design change?
Glass, aluminium and extra work can cost more than first planned.

Read whether prices can be changed when material costs rise and how the customer approves additional work. A larger contract value may simply cover extra materials or tasks rather than create more profit.
Is completed work turning into customer payment?
Recorded work can remain unbilled or unpaid.

Look at contract assets, meaning work not yet unconditionally billable, customer amounts due and retained payments. Compare them with cash generated by operations and investigate older balances or disputes.
Do factory work and site work stay in step?
Making panels early is not useful if they cannot be fitted.
Read production, deliveries and installation progress together. Check whether parts are waiting for the building to be ready and whether delays add storage, labour or transport costs.
Are defects and later obligations controlled?
Incorrect fitting or materials can require costly corrections.

Read warranty promises, customer claims and money set aside for expected costs. Check actual project requirements and testing rather than assuming a photograph of a finished building proves every quality claim.
risks: Building delays or financial problems can interrupt installation and payment.
Design changes, dearer materials and repeated work can reduce earnings under an agreed price.
Unapproved bills, old customer balances and retention can leave cash unavailable.
Unsafe work, defects or warranty repairs can cause delays, extra cost and claims.
context: The share sale funds a planned glass factory; the factory is not yet built

Glass Wall Systems’ shares began trading on 16 September 2026. Most shares sold in the offer came from existing owners, and that money went to them, not to the company. The smaller part, new shares issued by the company, is meant mainly to pay for a glass processing unit at its Vile Bhagad factory in Maharashtra. Backward integration means doing an earlier step yourself: here, cutting and preparing glass that it would otherwise buy ready-processed. Treat it as a plan until the company reports that the unit is built and running.
quiz: If exterior panels have been made in the factory, is the full job finished and paid for?
Not necessarily. They may still need delivery, installation, customer checks and release of payments held back under the contract.

financialNotes.title: The verified snapshot is a company total
financialNotes.text: The existing table uses standalone parent-company revenue and profit for the specified financial year. It does not establish separate revenue or profit for curtain walls, cladding, engineering or installation; those should not be invented from the offering list.

financialNotes.title: Read project cash alongside reported profit
financialNotes.text: Contract assets, receivables and retention can explain why earnings and cash move differently. Keep standalone and consolidated scope distinct and review the actual accounting policy before comparing project performance across periods.
